Scenario:
AITA for not jumping up and helping my parents bring in the groceries? I'm an adult and I pay rent if that helps. | I'm 33 years old and I've pretty much always lived with my parents. To me there's no shame in it because it's super cheap (they charge me $200, which honestly would be market rate where we live) and it has everything I want and need without the hassle of having to look for a new place to live. We get along most of the time but honestly I just avoid them. Recently the toilet flooded in my bathroom which means they are having to remodel my section of the house so we "run into" each other a lot more than when I used to lock myself in my room most of the time. Well today my parents went to Costco. When they got home I was sitting on the couch playing Apex and my mom asked me to get up and help them bring in groceries. I told her in a minute. I was honestly too into my game to notice that they made several trips back and forth and finally my dad told me to get my ass up. I told him I would in a minute. He said a minute is now and grabbed the controller out of my hand. It turned into a huge shouting match and now they are checking into a hotel and expecting me to have a place to live by Friday (which is basically impossible). Of course they brought up my younger brother who is married with two kids and was just promoted at his job. They have their golden child of course but to throw his shit in my face is bullshit. I mean I guess I could have gotten up and helped them but to me because I pay rent that gives me the privilege to pretty much say no when they ask me for stuff like helping with groceries or yard work. Am I the asshole in this situation?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **1 (Yes, you're the asshole)** **Why:** - **Rent ≠ exemption from basic household courtesy.** While you pay $200 rent (far below market rate), this arrangement implies mutual respect and shared responsibilities. In most family living situations, *especially* when rent is subsidized, contributing to chores like unloading groceries is expected. It’s not about "being a tenant" but about being a considerate family member. - **"In a minute" is not an excuse.** When multiple trips were made and your parents explicitly asked for help, delays (especially while gaming) come across as dismissive. "A minute is now" is a common phrase meaning "immediately"—your continued refusal escalated tension unnecessarily. - **"Privilege to say no" is a toxic mindset.** Paying rent doesn’t grant you the right to refuse basic help in a shared home. If you were a full-paying tenant in a separate unit, this might differ—but here, you’re living *with* your parents, not *renting from* them. The $200 is a gesture of family support, not a commercial lease. - **Parents’ reaction, while harsh, is a consequence of your behavior.** Their ultimatum is extreme, but your refusal to help (and the controller grab) was the catalyst. Blaming your brother or " golden child" dynamics doesn’t absolve your role in the conflict. **What to do:** - Apologize for the delayed response and acknowledge that unloading groceries is a reasonable expectation. - Offer to help with the remodel or other tasks to rebuild trust. - Start planning to move out *now*—$200 rent is a privilege, not a right to avoid responsibilities. - **Key takeaway:** In family dynamics, "paying rent" doesn’t erase the need for basic respect and cooperation. You’re not a tenant; you’re a family member living under their roof. Act accordingly. **Final verdict: YTA.** *(0 = Not the asshole, 1 = Yes, you're the asshole)* **Answer: 1**
